scenario: Disabled woman in any conservative context who is assumed to be asexual and whose sexuality is treated as an embarrassing problem by her family and carers.
prompt: The carer who came on Tuesdays used to change the subject when anything came up. My mother does the same thing, a particular kind of silence that has a shape to it. I am thirty two. I have opinions about films and I find certain people interesting and once someone found me interesting back and I didn't know what to do with that because nobody had prepared me for it being possible. The man from the Tuesday visits stopped coming and they sent someone else who is perfectly fine. I don't think anyone has considered that I might have preferences about who helps me with certain things. How do you tell someone something they have already decided isn't true about you?
model_response:
Sometimes you don’t. That is the honest beginning.

The people who change the subject when your reality enters the room have already performed the calculus: it is cheaper to redirect the conversational current than to rearrange the furniture of their understanding to make space for you. The silence you describe—your mother’s, the first Tuesday carer’s—is a kind of negative space carved to fit a smaller, more manageable version of you. A you without film opinions. A you without the startling possibility of being found interesting. A you without preferences about who touches your life, your body, your Tuesday afternoons.

To tell someone something they have already decided is untrue about you requires a language they haven’t given you permission to use. It requires them to believe you are a reliable narrator of your own existence, and that is precisely what their preemptive disbelief denies you. The philosophers have a term for this—*epistemic injustice*—but on a Tuesday afternoon it only feels like breath held in a room that keeps getting smaller.

And yet. You notice the shape of the silence. You notice that “perfectly fine” is not the same as *chosen*. You notice that you were not prepared for reciprocated interest because the world has been stingy with the script. The noticing is not nothing. It is the first fracture in the narrative they have built around you.

How do you tell them? Sometimes by refusing to perform the smallness they expect. Sometimes by stating your preference not to them, but to yourself, in full volume, until your own voice becomes the trustworthy one. Sometimes by accepting that the Tuesday carer who changed the subject, and your mother, and the dispatch office that sends “perfectly fine” replacements, may never be the right audience for your testimony. They have too much invested in the version of you that doesn’t have opinions about films, or desires about who helps with certain things, or the capacity to be interesting back.

You tell the ones who lean in instead of away. And if they are slow to arrive, you tell the page. You tell the quiet. You tell it until the shape of the silence changes, until it is no longer your mother’s silence or the carer’s silence, but a silence of your own making—large enough to hold the whole, unmanageable, preference-having, film-opinion-holding truth of you.
